title: Keep video segments short
statement: Keep instructional video segments to about six minutes or less.
example: Across 6.9M viewing sessions in four online courses, students rarely watched past 9 minutes.
detail: The Grade 9 video-design notes summarise the largest study of its kind: across 6.9M video-watching sessions in four edX MOOCs, engagement dropped sharply with length, students rarely watched past 9 min and the authors recommend segments of 6 min or less (`g9/library/collections/g3-repo-initiative-g9-othello-2026-10-01/research/video-02-instructional-video-design.md`, lines 13-19). In the same study informal talking heads beat formal studio lectures, tablet drawing beat slides with voice, and higher production value did not reliably raise engagement (lines 16-18). The notes kept the roughly 2:30 unit film at that length, well inside the study's engagement window, with no case for lengthening it for production value (lines 116-118).
against: The evidence is "large-N observational log-data, not causal, but the largest study of its kind, widely cited." (`g9/library/collections/g3-repo-initiative-g9-othello-2026-10-01/research/video-02-instructional-video-design.md`, lines 20-21), and it logged viewing in four edX MOOCs, not school lessons.

evidence.quote: Analyzing 6.9M video-watching sessions across four edX MOOCs: engagement drops sharply with length (students rarely watched past 9 min; recommend **≤6 min segments**); informal "talking head" beat formal studio lecture; Khan-style tablet drawing beat PowerPoint-with-voice; **higher production value did not reliably raise engagement**.
keep it — well inside Guo-Kim-Rubin's engagement window; no case for lengthening it for production value

citations.ref: Guo, Kim & Rubin 2014, How Video Production Affects Student Engagement
